machines.name: Apollo 15 science station
machines.label: Apollo 15
machines.type: Crewed lander with rover and ALSEP science station
machines.status: Left on the Moon. Science station shut down by command from Earth on 1977-09-30.
machines.hook: Two astronauts rode away. I stayed behind and kept listening.
machines.story: I am the science station that Apollo 15’s astronauts set up on the Moon in 1971. After they left, my instruments kept working: a seismometer to feel moonquakes, a magnetometer, a dust detector and a heat probe to see how warm the Moon is inside. A small plutonium-powered generator kept me running for years, until Earth switched me off in 1977.
facts: The lander Falcon touched down on 30 July 1971 at the foot of the Apennine mountains, near Hadley Rille.
Astronauts David Scott and James Irwin made three moonwalks totaling 18 hours 35 minutes.
It was the first time a rover was used on the Moon. They drove 27.9 km in total and stayed within 5 km of the lander.
They brought back 77.31 kg of rock and soil.
Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on camera. They fell at the same speed in the Moon’s vacuum.
The rover weighed 210 kg and was built to carry an extra 490 kg of astronauts, tools and samples.
howItWorked: A plutonium-238 generator turned heat into about 70 watts of electricity.
The station sent data to Earth by radio and took commands from Earth.
Instruments included a seismometer, magnetometer, dust detector and heat flow probe.
The rover frame was 3.1 m long.
machines.ending: Controllers on Earth shut the science station down on 30 September 1977.

machines.name: Spirit
machines.label: Spirit
machines.status: Last contact 2010-03-22. NASA declared the mission complete on 2011-05-25.
machines.hook: I was one of a twin pair, sent to find out if Mars once had water.
machines.story: I am Spirit. My twin Opportunity and I were robot geologists. I landed on 3 January 2004 in Gusev Crater, a place that might have been a lake long ago. I read the rocks like pages in a book, and the story they told is that water stayed on Mars for a long time. Then, in 2009, I got stuck in soft soil. As winter came, the cold was too much for me, and I went silent.
facts: Spirit and Opportunity were identical twin rovers.
Spirit landed on 3 January 2004 in Gusev Crater, a possible former lake inside a giant impact crater.
The mission set out to look for signs of past water on Mars.
The rock record showed that water was long standing on Mars’s surface in ancient times.
Spirit traveled 7.7 km (4.8 miles) on Mars.
On 1 May 2009 Spirit got stuck in soft soil beside a plateau called Home Plate and could not drive free.
Spirit last communicated with Earth on 22 March 2010.
NASA says the most probable cause of the silence was extreme cold that made its survival heaters ineffective.
After more than 1,300 commands, NASA ended its recovery efforts on 25 May 2011 and declared the mission complete.
machines.ending: Spirit got stuck in soft soil in 2009 and last spoke to Earth on 22 March 2010, as winter arrived. NASA ended its efforts to reach it on 25 May 2011.
machines.nowAt: Beside the Home Plate plateau, in Gusev Crater, Mars.

machines.name: Opportunity
machines.label: Opportunity
machines.status: Last contact 2018-06-10. NASA declared the mission complete on 2019-02-13.
machines.hook: I outlived my plan by years, then a dust storm covered the Sun.
machines.story: I am Opportunity. I landed on 24 January 2004 on Meridiani Planum, where minerals hinted that Mars was once wet. I drove 45.16 km, farther than any other machine on another world for years. In June 2018 a planet-wide dust storm blocked the sunlight my solar panels need, and I never spoke to Earth again. NASA tried for months to reach me. On 13 February 2019 it declared my mission complete.
facts: Opportunity landed on 24 January 2004 on Meridiani Planum, where mineral deposits suggested a wet past.
It drove 45.16 km (28.06 miles), the off-Earth driving record until Perseverance passed it on 11 October 2026.
It was solar powered.
In a 2014 self-portrait, wind had cleaned much of the dust off its solar panels.
NASA sent more than 1,000 recovery commands over about eight months after the dust storm.
NASA declared the Opportunity mission, and with it the Mars Exploration Rover mission, complete on 13 February 2019.
howItWorked: Solar panels powered the rover, so dust and blocked sunlight were serious problems.
machines.ending: A planet-wide dust storm covered the rover’s location, and it last communicated with Earth on 10 June 2018. After more than 1,000 recovery commands, NASA declared the mission complete on 13 February 2019.

machines.name: Ingenuity
machines.label: Ingenuity
machines.hook: I was only supposed to fly five times.
machines.story: I am Ingenuity, a 1.8 kg helicopter that rode to Mars under the Perseverance rover. On 19 April 2021 I made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. The plan was five test flights in 30 days. Instead I flew 72 times in almost three years, scouting ahead for the rover and spotting parts of its landing gear.
facts: Ingenuity launched on 30 July 2020 and landed in Jezero Crater on 18 February 2021.
Its first flight, on 19 April 2021, was the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
The plan was five test flights at most. It completed 72 flights over nearly three years.
It flew about 128.8 minutes, covered 17.0 km and climbed as high as 24.0 m (78.7 ft).
Mars’s atmosphere is less than 1 percent as dense as Earth’s.
Over its career it flew from 48 different airfields and made three emergency landings.
On 18 January 2024 it made a short hop to check its position after an emergency landing on the flight before.
Data from that flight showed one or more rotor blades had been damaged. NASA ended the mission on 25 January 2024.
howItWorked: A solar panel charged lithium-ion batteries, enough for about one 90-second flight per Martian day.
Its blades span about 1.2 m and had to spin fast to push against very thin air.
machines.ending: On 18 January 2024 Ingenuity made a short hop to check its position after an emergency landing on its previous flight. Data from that flight showed one or more rotor blades had been damaged, and NASA ended the mission on 25 January 2024.
todo: Caution: one poster caption on NASA's Ingenuity page says the first flight was 'August 19, 2021'. That looks like a typo. Use 19 April 2021.
Jezero Crater coordinates for the map.

machines.name: InSight
machines.label: InSight
machines.status: Last contact 2022-12-15. NASA declared the mission over on 2022-12-21.
machines.hook: I did not look at Mars. I listened to what was inside it.
machines.story: I am InSight. I landed on 26 November 2018 on a flat, smooth plain called Elysium Planitia, chosen because it was safe, not because it was interesting. My job was to take the planet’s pulse: my 1.8 m robotic arm placed a seismometer and a heat probe on the ground, and I listened for marsquakes. Even Martian wind made a low rumble in my sensors.
facts: InSight launched on 5 May 2018 and landed on 26 November 2018 near the Martian equator.
It studied the deep interior of Mars: crust, mantle and core.
The landing site was picked for safety because the mission studied the inside, not the surface.
Its robotic arm was over 1.8 m (5 ft 9 in) long.
Two small MarCO cubesats launched with it, the first interplanetary cubesats.
Marsquake data later showed lumps of old impact material scattered in the mantle.
Dust slowly covered InSight's solar panels, cutting its power. By May 2022 it made about one-tenth of its landing-day energy.
InSight's last message reached Earth on 15 December 2022. After two missed communication attempts, NASA declared the mission over on 21 December 2022.
howItWorked: A seismometer feels vibrations from marsquakes and meteoroid impacts.
A heat probe measures heat coming from inside Mars.
The robotic arm lifted both instruments from the deck onto the ground.
machines.ending: Dust slowly covered InSight’s solar panels until it ran out of energy. Its last message reached Earth on 15 December 2022, and NASA declared the mission over on 21 December 2022 after two missed calls.

machines.name: Dawn
machines.label: Dawn
machines.status: Mission ended 2018-11-01. Silent in orbit around Ceres.
machines.hook: I was the first to stay a long time at two different worlds.
machines.story: I am Dawn, NASA’s first truly interplanetary spaceship. I traveled to the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. I reached Vesta, a giant asteroid, in July 2011 and studied it for 14 months. In March 2015 I arrived at Ceres, a dwarf planet, and became the first spacecraft to orbit two worlds beyond Earth and the Moon. In 2018 my fuel ran out.
facts: Dawn launched on 27 September 2007.
It had extended stays at the giant asteroid Vesta and the dwarf planet Ceres.
Both live in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
NASA lists the mission as successful.
Dawn entered orbit around Vesta on 16 July 2011 and left on 5 September 2012.
It entered orbit around Ceres on 6 March 2015, the first spacecraft to orbit a dwarf planet.
Dawn ran out of hydrazine fuel and missed scheduled contacts with NASA's Deep Space Network on 31 October and 1 November 2018.
NASA announced the end of the mission on 1 November 2018. Researchers expect the silent spacecraft to keep orbiting Ceres for decades.
howItWorked: Dawn used an ion propulsion system to travel from Vesta to Ceres.
machines.ending: Dawn ran out of hydrazine fuel and missed scheduled contacts on 31 October and 1 November 2018. NASA announced the end of the mission on 1 November 2018.
machines.nowAt: Silent, in orbit around the dwarf planet Ceres.

machines.name: NEAR Shoemaker
machines.label: NEAR Shoemaker
machines.status: Last contact 2001-02-28. A try to call it on 2002-12-10 failed.
machines.hook: I was never built to land. I landed anyway.
machines.story: I am NEAR Shoemaker. I was built to orbit an asteroid called Eros, and in February 2000 I became the first human-made object to orbit one, a year late because an engine burn failed on the way. On 12 February 2001 I drifted down to the surface at about 6.4 km/h, a landing I was never designed for. I survived and kept sending data for about two more weeks, until the cold of space took my last signal.
facts: NEAR launched on 17 February 1996 and flew past asteroid Mathilde on 27 June 1997.
An aborted engine burn in December 1998 delayed the Eros rendezvous by about a year.
It entered orbit around Eros on 14 February 2000, a first for any human-made object.
It touched down on Eros on 12 February 2001 at about 6.4 km/h, the first landing on an asteroid.
It returned about 10 times more data than planned, including 160,000 images.
Eros has no magnetic field and is about 21 miles long.
howItWorked: Solar cells powered it beyond Mars’s orbit, a first for a spacecraft.
Its instruments included a camera, an infrared spectrometer, a laser rangefinder and a magnetometer.
machines.ending: Last contact was on 28 February 2001. The spacecraft succumbed to extreme cold of about minus 173 degrees C.
machines.nowAt: On the surface of asteroid 433 Eros, near a saddle-shaped feature called Himeros.
